profiles.name: Pat McGeehan
profiles.excerpt: Pat McGeehan combined acting with announcing and narration, becoming a long-running Red Skelton foil while also leading detective drama and narrating major network programs.
profiles.bio_html:
Patrick McGeehan came to broadcasting after an adventurous start far from the studio. Born in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in 1907, he went to sea as a teenager, spent years traveling, and later worked in vaudeville and musical comedy. He entered radio in the mid-1930s and developed the versatility that the network era rewarded, moving between straight acting, narration and announcing.

McGeehan's microphone career included Ben Calvert on Aunt Mary, narration for Ceiling Unlimited, and the title detective in The Adventures of Bill Lance. His longest public association was with Red Skelton. He joined Skelton's radio program as an announcer in the 1940s, became one of the announcers used as a comic foil, and also handled incidental acting. That combination makes announcing and narration a genuine second branch of his GRH identity rather than a minor credit.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 87 The Red Skelton Show performances credited to McGeehan, eight Roy Rogers appearances, six Let George Do It performances and additional work on The Whistler, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, Dr. Christian, Gunsmoke and Jeff Regan, Investigator.

profiles.name: William Redfield
profiles.excerpt: William Redfield grew from a Broadway child actor into a mature radio repertory performer, with X Minus One and CBS Radio Mystery Theater forming a substantial late chapter of his career.
profiles.bio_html:
William Redfield began acting professionally as a child in New York. He made his Broadway debut at nine and appeared in the original Broadway production of Our Town while still young. Stage work remained central throughout his life, but radio gave him another durable arena for character acting from the 1940s through the final years of his career.

Redfield's radio work crossed several generations of network drama. In the 1950s he appeared repeatedly on X Minus One and later worked on Theater Five, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar and CBS Radio Workshop. When CBS Radio Mystery Theater revived regular network drama in 1974, Redfield became one of its busiest repertory actors. At the same time his stage and screen career continued, including his memorable role as Dale Harding in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 77 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances, 11 Theater Five appearances, nine X Minus One episodes, eight Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances and additional work on CBS Radio Workshop, Have Gun, Will Travel, Stroke of Fate and Words at War.

profiles.name: Staats Cotsworth
profiles.excerpt: Staats Cotsworth turned from a serious career in visual art to radio acting and became the definitive Casey, Crime Photographer, while continuing to work in drama for decades.
profiles.bio_html:
Staats Cotsworth trained first as an artist, studying in the United States and in Paris and exhibiting his work before the Depression made a living from painting harder to sustain. He turned toward the theatre, joined Eva Le Gallienne's Civic Repertory Theatre, and discovered that his voice opened another professional path in radio.

By the late 1930s Cotsworth was working regularly at the microphone, but the role that defined his radio career was newspaper photographer and amateur sleuth Casey. He became the best-remembered star of Casey, Crime Photographer, giving the character a combination of newsroom toughness and curiosity that carried the series through much of its network run. He continued working after Casey in anthology and science-fiction drama and later joined the repertory of CBS Radio Mystery Theater.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 71 Casey, Crime Photographer performances, nine CBS Radio Mystery Theater appearances, five The Chase episodes, four each on CBS Radio Workshop and Theater Five, three Dimension X performances, three Inspector Thorne episodes and three Words at War appearances.

profiles.name: Edwin Max
profiles.excerpt: Edwin Max was a Hollywood character actor with a substantial parallel radio career, including first mate Gallagher on Voyage of the Scarlet Queen and years of Lux repertory work.
profiles.bio_html:
Edwin Max, born in Georgia in 1909 and credited early in his screen career as Edwin Miller, built his profession as a character actor rather than as a celebrity lead. His film work stretched from the late 1930s through the 1970s and included crime pictures, westerns and supporting dramatic roles. Radio developed alongside that screen career and gave his distinctive voice much more room to work.

His strongest continuing radio role was Gallagher, first mate to Elliott Lewis's Captain Philip Carney on Voyage of the Scarlet Queen. Max also became a dependable member of the Hollywood dramatic pool heard on Lux Radio Theatre, where he could move from named supporting characters to smaller parts around each week's stars. His range can be heard in the 1950 Lux adaptation of The Wizard of Oz, where he played Zeke and the Cowardly Lion.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 32 Voyage of the Scarlet Queen performances, 25 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, eight Wild Bill Hickok appearances, six Broadway Is My Beat episodes and additional work on Screen Directors Playhouse, The Whistler, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar and Night Beat.

profiles.name: Jim Boles
profiles.excerpt: Jim Boles became the postwar Doc Long on I Love a Mystery, carrying one of radio adventure's best-known characters through the New York revival while building a broader stage and broadcast career.
profiles.bio_html:
Jim Boles was born in Lubbock, Texas in 1914 and began his professional career in radio. He became a familiar supporting voice across network programs, but his defining microphone role arrived when Carlton E. Morse revived I Love a Mystery in New York in 1949.

Boles took over Doc Long, the drawling Texan adventurer previously played by Barton Yarborough, opposite Russell Thorson's Jack Packard and Tony Randall's Reggie York. The revival returned to Morse's earlier serial stories, giving Boles years of continuing work in a role that demanded comedy, action and supernatural suspense. Away from the microphone, Boles also built a long stage and television career and became known for repeatedly portraying Abraham Lincoln.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 84 I Love a Mystery performances credited to Boles, four Words at War appearances, four X Minus One episodes, four Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances and two John Steele, Adventurer appearances. His GRH holdings make Doc Long the clear center of his radio biography without reducing his career to that single character.

profiles.name: Portland Hoffa
profiles.excerpt: Portland Hoffa was not simply Fred Allen's wife on the air. Her high, deliberate delivery and comic timing made her the indispensable straight woman at the center of his radio world for nearly two decades.
profiles.bio_html:
Portland Hoffa was born in Portland, Oregon in 1905 and built a stage career as a dancer before radio became her principal medium. She worked on Broadway in the 1920s and met Fred Allen while both were appearing in The Passing Show of 1922. Their marriage became a professional partnership as well, but Hoffa entered broadcasting with her own stage experience and a voice that was instantly recognizable.

Allen and Hoffa began their radio career together in 1932 on The Linit Bath Club Revue. Across the programs that followed, Hoffa's lilting delivery and apparently innocent questions gave Allen the setup for some of his sharpest lines. Her familiar exchanges with him became part of the show's sound, and her contribution depended on precision: the straight line had to land exactly right for Allen's reply to work. She remained a regular through the end of his network series and later joined him on appearances such as The Big Show.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 87 The Fred Allen Show performances and 11 The Big Show appearances credited to Hoffa. Those holdings document a radio partnership in which her voice and timing were structural parts of the comedy rather than decorative additions to her husband's program.

profiles.name: Will Wright
profiles.excerpt: Will Wright brought a newspaperman's ear and decades of stage experience to thousands of radio broadcasts, becoming one of Hollywood radio's most prolific character voices before his screen career made his face familiar.
profiles.bio_html:
William Henry Wright was born in San Francisco in 1894 and worked as a newspaperman before turning to show business. Vaudeville and stage acting gave him a foundation, but radio became one of the largest parts of his professional life. Contemporary accounts and later reference works credit him with appearing in thousands of broadcasts.

Wright's radio career was built on character work. He played recurring roles such as Zeb on Al Pearce and His Gang, George Honeywell on My Little Margie, Mahoney on Glamour Manor, and the title lawyer in The Amazing Mr. Tutt. His dry, often irritable delivery also made him ideal for westerns and detective drama. Screen audiences later knew that same character presence from more than 200 film and television roles, while Disney listeners heard him as Friend Owl in Bambi.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 55 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances, 22 A Man Called X appearances, six The Six Shooter episodes and additional work on Gunsmoke, Tales of the Texas Rangers, The Great Gildersleeve, Dr. Kildare and Frontier Gentleman.

profiles.name: Norman Field
profiles.excerpt: Norman Field was one of Lux Radio Theatre's dependable character specialists, a veteran stage and radio actor whose command of the medium also led him to teach radio drama in Los Angeles.
profiles.bio_html:
Norman Field came to radio after a long stage apprenticeship. By 1946, a contemporary profile described him as having begun his stage career roughly three decades earlier and having worked steadily in radio for about fifteen years. That experience made him valuable in Hollywood, where anthology productions needed actors who could establish age, profession and social position with only a few lines.

Lux Radio Theatre became the strongest surviving record of Field's work. A 1946 Radio Life feature described him as a fixture in the Lux supporting company and singled out his ability to play bankers, businessmen, doctors, family lawyers and Wall Street figures. He also taught radio drama through the UCLA extension program, turning practical studio experience into instruction for other performers.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 63 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, five Encore Theater appearances, five NBC University Theater performances, four each on Screen Directors Playhouse and The Whistler, three Dr. Christian episodes, three Mystery Is My Hobby appearances and two Richard Diamond, Private Detective performances.

profiles.name: Jack Grimes
profiles.excerpt: Jack Grimes was a working radio actor from childhood, moving from dozens of weekly juvenile assignments to Jimmy Olsen on Superman and later becoming a major CBS Radio Mystery Theater repertory voice.
profiles.bio_html:
Jack Grimes began acting at seven during the Depression, helping support his family while attending the Professional Children's School in New York. Radio quickly became a demanding profession rather than an occasional child-actor job. By age twelve he was reportedly appearing on 35 to 40 broadcasts a week while also building stage experience.

Grimes grew into adult radio without leaving the medium behind. He played Jimmy Olsen during the final years of The Adventures of Superman radio series, worked on programs such as Let's Pretend and The Fred Allen Show, and later became part of the repertory that powered Theater Five and CBS Radio Mystery Theater. His voice career continued into animation, including Sparky and Chim-Chim on the English-language version of Speed Racer.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 40 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances, 30 Theater Five appearances, eight X Minus One episodes, eight Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances, five Columbia Workshop appearances, two Dimension X episodes and additional work on Casey, Crime Photographer and Dr. Christian.

profiles.name: Michael Ann Barrett
profiles.excerpt: Michael Ann Barrett was a busy West Coast radio actress whose surviving work crosses private-eye drama, westerns and suspense, with major GRH holdings in Frank Race, Johnny Dollar, Gunsmoke and Philip Marlowe.
profiles.bio_html:
Michael Ann Barrett was born in New York City in 1922 and built a professional acting career that included radio, film and television. Her screen credits were largely supporting parts, but radio gave her a much broader body of work, especially in the West Coast dramatic companies that supplied detectives, westerns and anthology programs with new characters every week.

Barrett's microphone career shows the value of that repertory skill. She worked repeatedly on The Adventures of Frank Race, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe, Gunsmoke, Escape and The Whistler. Rather than being tied to a single signature role, she moved among victims, suspects, wives, witnesses and frontier characters as the scripts required. Her later television work included appearances on Dragnet and other dramatic series.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 16 The Adventures of Frank Race performances, 14 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, nine each on Gunsmoke and The Adventures of Philip Marlowe, eight Broadway Is My Beat episodes, seven each on Escape and Tales of the Texas Rangers, and six The Whistler performances.
